speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: Step out of the kennel, Master Shakespeare, or you will carry half the close onto the flags.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: The frost is out of the stones, Mistress, and the mud is very willing.

speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: Willing or no, it stays outside the porch. Gillis, pull your cloak about your throat. That east wind comes straight off the ditch.

speaker: gillis_verbeke
text: I have my wool beneath, Mistress Ansell. It is a good weight for March.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: Good morrow, Mistress Ansell. Good morrow, neighbours. You are early for the first Sunday in Lent, which is a comfortable sign in a cold parish.

speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: We keep hours in my house, Master Thwaite, whether the playhouses are shut or open.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: When the playhouses are shut, the pews have room to breathe. Have you your voice after Wednesday's commination, Master Shakespeare?

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: Whole and quiet, sir. It has had its rest since Shrove Tuesday, which is more than my knees will get this morning.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: The knees were made for Lent, sir. I have divided the epistle into fourteen heads today, that no man may go to his salt herring unexamined.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: Fourteen is a very thorough measure, Master Thwaite.

speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: Twelve would serve, if the twelfth were aimed at the apprentices in the back alley. They were singing after nine on Friday night.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: My eleventh head touches upon unseasonable mirth, Mistress Ansell, and my fourteenth upon the reckoning every house must make before Easter.

speaker: gillis_verbeke
text: We have no singing in the back room, sir. Only the loom till dusk, and the shuttle makes a small noise.

speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: Gillis makes less noise with four treadles than a player makes walking across a floor above my head.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: I had my shoes off by eight last night, Mistress.

speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: Then you think heavier in Lent than you did at Shrovetide, for the joists knew all about it.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: What is it you read so late in the fast, Master Shakespeare? Some godly homily, I trust.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: An old moral poem, sir, wherein young folk are counselled to obey their parents and beware of haste.

speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: A sixpenny book out of Paul's, with the last leaf gone, and my grey cat asleep on the best half of it. I saw it when I counted the candle-ends.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: See the moral outlast the candle. Sixpence the week for firing and washing, till Lady Day, and Mistress Ansell will not let you freeze over it.

speaker: dorcas_ansell
text: The sixpence runs till Lady Day, and then the sun may warm him for nothing. I shall still want quiet after nine.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: You shall have it, Mistress.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: I turn the glass twice on a Sunday in Lent. The second turning is where a man remembers he is still in the porch of the matter.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: I will still be awake for it, sir.

speaker: gillis_verbeke
text: I take the bench by the pillar, Master Shakespeare.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: Go on, Gillis. Leave me the draughty end.

speaker: josias_thwaite
text: Mark the fourteenth head, Master Shakespeare. It is the hinge of the whole.

speaker: william_shakespeare
text: I never miss a fourteenthly, sir.
